claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection in noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and kinetically limited diffusion.
High configurational entropy favors formation or retention of a single-phase solid solution.
Excessively rapid heating or cooling prevents adequate interdiffusion and homogenization of the multielement precursors.
Inadequate interdiffusion causes phase separation or elemental segregation.
Tuning thermal ramp rates and peak-temperature dwell time can provide sufficient atomic mobility while trapping a single phase before decomposition or secondary-phase growth.
The target composition can ideally form an fcc-like or bcc-like single-phase solid solution.
Heating rate, cooling rate, and peak-temperature dwell time should be varied while composition and reaction environment are held fixed.
Relevant processing conditions include peak temperatures around 1100–1200 K and dwell times from milliseconds to several minutes.
The relevant processing atmosphere is inert or reducing.
Elemental interdiffusion and mixing efficiency, relative to the entropic drive toward a random solution, is the structural mediator between the thermal history and the final phase.
Local kinetic barriers can induce phase segregation.
Moderate, well-chosen heating and cooling profiles favor a single-phase solid solution over both more rapid and slower profiles.
An optimized dwell can avoid unintended nanoparticle coalescence or agglomeration.
Intermediate ramp rates and controlled dwell times will predominantly produce a single-phase random alloy with a uniform elemental distribution.
Overly fast or overly slow thermal ramps will produce detectable secondary phases or localized elemental inhomogeneities.
A validated rapid-thermal route can provide a single-phase nanoparticle baseline with minimal segregation.
The hypothesis applies specifically to nearly equiatomic mixtures of six or more noble metals processed at 1100–1200 K under inert or reducing conditions.
Consistent formation of a stable single phase across the examined range of ramp rates and dwell times would falsify the proposed dependence on a specific time–temperature protocol.
